description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de nivel medio superior apasionados por la tecnología, la ciencia y la exploración espacial. Combinando nuestras ganas de aprender y nuestra curiosidad, estamos desarrollando proyectos para explorar y acercarnos al mundo de la ciencia de datos y la inteligencia artificial, demostrando que desde el bachillerato se pueden crear grandes cosas
summary:
Project Summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten
What was developed:
An interactive educational telerobotic platform connected to a physical rover at CECyTE Plantel 04 Ayala in Tlayecac, Morelos, Mexico. It integrates an ESP32-S3-CAM microcontroller, live video streaming via an OV3660 camera, an RFID reader, Mecanum wheels, a PHP/MySQL cloud architecture for secure turn-based remote control, and a physical lunar/Martian terrain featuring student artwork hiding RFID tags.

How it addresses the challenge:
It transforms the history of discarded space missions (like Luna 2, Apollo 11, Viking 1, Opportunity, and Lunar Retroreflectors) into an active remote exploration experience. Users worldwide pilot the robot over the internet using a live camera feed, navigating obstacles to symbolically "rescue" historical relics. Scanning an RFID tag triggers instant web notifications, voice narration, and digital return animations.

Why it is important:

Democratization: Enables students in rural Morelos and globally to operate advanced robotics, IoT, and computer vision remotely and for free.

Preservation: Combines STEM and student art to keep the legacy of space pioneers alive and spark technological vocations.

Global Impact: Proves that public schools in Mexico can build functional, low-cost telerobotic stations connecting local classrooms to the world.
details:
Project Details: Abandoned but Not Forgotten

What does it do and how does it work? It is an interactive, educational telerobotic platform that allows any user, from anywhere in the world, to control in real time a physical exploratory rover located at the ground station in Tlayecac, Morelos, Mexico (CECyTE Plantel 04 Ayala).

  1. Turn-Based Access and Control: The user requests credentials on the web portal and automatically receives their username and password via email. A turn management system assigns exclusive control of the physical robot to one pilot at a time to prevent collisions or server congestion.
  2. Navigation with Live Vision: Through a web interface featuring omnidirectional controls (10 movements and PWM power adjustment), the pilot observes the real-time video stream from the rover's integrated camera while driving it across a physical mockup of the lunar and Martian surface.
  3. Search, RFID Detection, and Web Notification: The primary objective of the robot is to search for the forgotten historical object (represented physically by an artistic drawing and a hidden RFID tag). When the rover approaches and scans the RFID card with its front antenna, the system checks whether it matches the mission's target object. Upon confirmation, the vehicle stops automatically, a real-time alert is sent to the web page indicating that the artifact has been found, and a child-friendly voice narration detailing its scientific history is triggered alongside a digital animation of its symbolic return to Earth.

What benefits does it offer?

  • Remote and free access to real robotics: Eliminates the need for expensive hardware at home or in the classroom; any student with an internet connection can operate a physical robot thousands of miles away.
  • Multisensory learning (STEM + Art): Combines robotic engineering, web programming, voice-assisted reading, and student-created visual arts, facilitating the understanding of space concepts for children and young people.
  • Safe and orderly operation: Its client-server architecture with single-session control and speed regulation protects the mechanical integrity of the physical prototype against multiple simultaneous connections.

What is the expected impact of the project?

  • Democratizing space science from Mexico: Enables children and youths from rural communities in Morelos and from any country to experience firsthand how a planetary rover is operated with real-time latency and remote vision.
  • Preserving space technology memory: Prevents the early robotic explorers of the Moon and Mars from being forgotten, turning historical data into relatable stories that spark scientific and technological vocations.
  • Projecting Mexican student talent: Demonstrates that from a public school in Mexico, it is possible to develop low-cost, functional telerobotic stations with global reach.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

  • Hardware and Electronics: ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 DevKitC-1 N16R8 microcontroller (featuring WiFi, BLE 5 connectivity, and OPI PSRAM memory), integrated OV3660 camera with USB-C interface for MJPEG streaming, MFRC522 RFID reader module with passive cards/tags, dual-channel H-bridge for PWM control, 4 TT gear motors with Mecanum omnidirectional wheels, 3D-printed chassis, and a physical mockup featuring student artwork.
  • Firmware and Embedded Languages: C / C++ in Arduino IDE, utilizing libraries such as esp_camera.h, WiFiClientSecure.h, HTTPClient.h, WebServer.h, MFRC522.h, and concurrent tasks in FreeRTOS (separating the video streaming core from the telemetry and control loop).
  • Web Development, Backend, and Database: HTML5, CSS3 (Tailwind CSS), JavaScript (ES6+), PHP 8, and MySQL (hosted on a cloud server for command synchronization, RFID telemetry logging, finding validation, and automated email credential dispatch).
  • Multimedia and User Experience: HTML5 Canvas (for the return animation of Moon/Mars probes to Earth), Web Speech API (speechSynthesis) for real-time voice narration, GSAP, tsParticles, and Canvas Confetti.

Where does the creativity of the project lie? The creativity lies in uniting the physical world, student art, and telerobotics into an interactive story: instead of building a purely virtual simulator or a local exhibition robot, we turn hand-drawn artwork by Mexican students into physical narrative portals via hidden RFID tags. The user does not merely drive a remote-controlled car; they star in a rescue mission where the robot actively explores the environment, recognizes the target via wireless telemetry, and notifies its success on the web interface, bridging the gap between aerospace engineering and artistic imagination.

What factors did the team take into account?

  • Security and user concurrency: A temporary exclusivity system was designed in the database so that only one user controls the rover at a time, automatically releasing the turn after a period of inactivity.
  • Hardware stability and energy efficiency: The ESP32-S3 pins were optimized to prevent conflicts with the Octal PSRAM memory and the integrated OV3660 camera, separating the video server into an independent thread (streamTask) so that the video feed does not interrupt motor response or RFID reading.
  • Accessibility and inclusiveness: Automatic voice narration, large touch buttons for mobile devices, immediate visual feedback, and bilingual support were incorporated so that both young children and international visitors can interact without technical barriers.
